title: Many schools
hook: Catholic thought also has Bonaventure, Scotus and many others; the Church keeps several schools

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fossanova: Thomas, on the road to a council, taken in by Cistercian monks, and dying in their care. Your line was the angelic doctor. Which teacher did you thank? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

After a whole block of days with one teacher, it's fair to wonder: is Thomas Aquinas simply what Catholics think? Is the Summa the official answer key, and everyone else a footnote? The shelves of a Catholic university library tell another story. Next to Thomas sit Augustine, from long before. Bonaventure, a Franciscan who taught in Paris in Thomas's own time. John Duns Scotus, another Franciscan, who argued with Thomas's ideas after Thomas was gone. And more besides. Today: many schools.
screen: `IS THOMAS THE ANSWER KEY?` → `THE SHELVES SAY OTHERWISE.` → `AUGUSTINE, BONAVENTURE, SCOTUS.`

segments.voice: A school, in this sense, isn't a building. It's a way of thinking that teachers hand down to students, generation after generation. Thomists follow Thomas. Scotists follow Scotus. Others draw mainly on Augustine, or on Bonaventure. Each school has its favorite questions and its own instincts, its own way of putting God, the soul and the world together. And here's the surprising part. The Catholic Church has praised Thomas very highly and recommended him to students for the priesthood. But it has not made him the only teacher. On many questions, the Church lets these schools disagree, out loud and in print, without naming a winner. Their students argue in classrooms and stay at the same altar. That's just how Thomas wrote, too. Remember how the Summa works: state the other side first, and state it fairly. The objection always gets its say before the answer. A school that learned from Thomas has to be ready to listen to a school that didn't. Paul saw the early version of this. In Corinth, people were lining up behind their favorite teachers, one for Paul, one for Apollo. Paul's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase." Teachers are gardeners. None of them owns the garden. So as this block closes, look back at what Thomas gave: a boy who kept his call, an argument that states the other side, grace that completes, God holding the world now, habits that make us, a lamp that lights others, and straw next to what he saw. One teacher, and many beside him.
screen: `A SCHOOL IS A WAY OF THINKING.` · `PRAISED, BUT NOT THE ONLY ONE.` · `ARGUE IN CLASS, SHARE THE ALTAR.` · `TEACHERS ARE GARDENERS.` · then, large: `GOD GAVE THE INCREASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from a different school. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a way of seeing things that isn't your usual one. A writer you'd never pick up. A friend whose instincts run the other way. A tradition in your own family you've quietly tuned out. Don't argue with it yet. Just ask: what might this teacher see that I've been missing? Let one thing come. If you pray, you can ask God to plant, water, or grow something through a voice you'd never have chosen. The bell holds the time.
Many schools. Thomists, Scotists, followers of Augustine and Bonaventure: ways of Catholic thinking the Church keeps side by side, without making any one of them the only teacher. Today's word.
Your line: many teachers. Today, read or listen to one paragraph from someone outside your usual school, and find one thing worth keeping. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Catholic universities and seminaries teach Thomas alongside Augustine, Bonaventure, Scotus and others, and theologians from different schools can debate open questions in print and in class.

notes: No count of days spoken ('a whole block of days').

Church recommending Thomas for priestly formation: paraphrased from Optatam Totius 16 and canon 252 §3 ('with St. Thomas as teacher'); 'never made him the only teacher' and 'lets these schools disagree without naming a winner' to be confirmed by a Keeper.
Bonaventure taught in Paris in Thomas's time; Scotus later engaged Thomas's positions. Confirm phrasing. These figures get their own days (1218–1220), so they are only named here.
'Original' left null: no single original-language word fits the day.
Editor pass: 'has never made him the only teacher' (an absolute the cited documents don't state) softened to 'has not', in voice and screen; howItsDone's 'still debate' claim softened.
